opus-5.5.text:
I think the knowledge base is really the foundation that everything else stands on. When you look at how human mathematicians work, nobody proves a deep theorem from the axioms up. You stand on centuries of accumulated results: definitions, lemmas, standard techniques, the "folklore" everyone in a field just knows. A formal system like Lean is the same, except that everything has to be made explicit. If the library doesn't contain the right definition of a scheme, or the right version of some compactness lemma, then the model can be brilliant at reasoning and still get stuck, because it has to rebuild huge amounts of infrastructure before it can even state the problem.

So there are a few layers to why it matters. First, coverage. Mathlib is an incredible community effort, but it still covers only a fraction of research-level mathematics. If you want AI to work on frontier problems, someone or something has to formalize far more of the underlying theory. That's partly an autoformalization challenge, translating textbooks and papers into formal statements and proofs at scale.

Second, retrieval and reuse. Even when a lemma exists, the system has to find it. A good knowledge base isn't just a pile of theorems. It's organized, with consistent naming and abstractions designed so that results compose well. That's what makes proof search tractable, rather than the model wandering through millions of possibilities.

Third, it compounds. Every proof the system verifies can go back into the library, so the knowledge base grows, and the next problem becomes easier. That flywheel is something you don't get from informal reasoning alone, because an informal proof might have a subtle gap, and if you build on it, errors propagate. With formal verification, every brick you add is guaranteed sound, so you can keep building higher without worrying the tower will collapse.

And finally, it's about trust. As AI systems produce more and more mathematics, humans won't be able to check everything line by line. A verified, shared knowledge base becomes the common ground: the place where results are certified and where humans and AI can collaborate. In a sense, I see it as building the infrastructure for the future of mathematics itself, not just a tool for one model.

r001.rationale: It says Mathlib covers only a fraction of research-level mathematics and that missing theory can leave a system stuck.

r002.rationale: It discusses retrieval and reuse of existing lemmas, but does not say that searching known results can uncover a counterexample to refute a claim.

r003.rationale: It describes autoformalization as translating textbooks and papers into formal statements and proofs, but does not distinguish that conversion from proving mathematical claims.

fable-5.1.text:
Because formal mathematics, unlike natural-language mathematics, has an unforgiving dependency structure. When a mathematician writes a paper, they can say "by a standard compactness argument" and every reader fills in the gap. When you write a proof in Lean, there is no filling in gaps. Every object you reference has to already exist in the library, with exactly the right definition, and every lemma you invoke has to already be proven and stated in a form you can actually apply. So the question "can the model prove this theorem" is really two questions. Does the model know how to reason, and does the library contain the building blocks the reasoning needs?

For a long time people focused only on the first question, and I think that was a mistake. If you give a very strong model a research-level problem and the surrounding definitions simply aren't formalized, the model is stuck no matter how clever it is. It's like asking someone to build a house and not giving them bricks. Mathlib is wonderful, but it still covers a surprisingly narrow slice of what working mathematicians actually use, and it's very uneven across fields. Large parts of analysis, PDE, algebraic geometry, and probability are thin or missing. So in practice, when we look at why a proof attempt fails, it's often not that the model made a logical error. It's that it needed a lemma that didn't exist, or the version that existed was stated for the wrong generality, or the definition in the library didn't match the one in the paper.

The second reason is retrieval. Even when the right lemma exists, there are now hundreds of thousands of declarations in Mathlib, and names like `Measure.ae_eq_of_forall_setLIntegral_eq` are not something you can guess. A model with no structured access to the library ends up hallucinating plausible-sounding lemma names, and then wastes its whole search budget on things that don't compile. So the knowledge base is not just a static pile of theorems. It needs to be something the model can search over semantically, where it can ask "is there anything that relates this norm bound to this integral" and get back the real statements.

And then the third piece, which I think is the most interesting, is that the knowledge base has to grow as a byproduct of the system working. When the model proves an intermediate lemma on the way to something larger, that lemma should be kept, checked, deduplicated, and made available next time. That's how human mathematics accumulates. Nobody re-proves the fundamental theorem of calculus every time. If the system doesn't do that, every problem starts from zero and you never get compounding returns. If it does, the hard problems slowly become easy ones, because the distance from the library to the frontier keeps shrinking.

So that's really why I see it as central. The reasoning engine gets a lot of attention because it's the glamorous part, but the knowledge base is what determines whether the reasoning engine ever gets to touch the actual frontier of mathematics, or just keeps solving competition problems in a vacuum.

r001.rationale: It says Mathlib covers a surprisingly narrow and uneven slice of working mathematics, with large areas thin or missing, so models can lack needed formalized definitions and lemmas.

r002.rationale: It discusses searching for existing lemmas, but does not explain that searching known results can uncover a counterexample to refute a claim.

r003.rationale: It does not mention autoformalization or distinguish converting mathematics into formal representations from proving claims.

astra-6.text:
A formal proof doesn’t happen in isolation. It builds on definitions, lemmas, and theorems that have already been established. So an AI needs more than the ability to reason through a few steps; it needs access to the right mathematical knowledge at the right time.

A knowledge base gives it that foundation. The challenge is finding a result whose precise assumptions match the problem you’re working on. Something that looks relevant in ordinary mathematical language may have a formal statement that requires additional conditions.

If the system can retrieve and apply those results effectively, it can build on existing work instead of repeatedly proving everything from scratch. The proof checker still verifies correctness, but the knowledge base helps the AI find a path to a proof.

sol-6.1.text:
A formal proof has to connect every step to precise definitions and results that have already been established. So a knowledge base gives the AI the mathematical material it can actually use: definitions, lemmas, theorems, and the relationships between them.

The challenge is that having those results stored somewhere isn’t enough. The system has to find the right result, recognize that it applies, and satisfy its assumptions. A useful knowledge base helps bridge the gap between a high-level idea—“this follows from a standard theorem”—and the exact statement a proof assistant can check.

It also makes progress cumulative. Once a result has been formally verified, later proofs can build on it instead of deriving everything from first principles.
